checklistItems.text: Provide information about risk and behaviour change in a non-judgemental way
Provide information about risk, behaviour change and early detection in plain language
Ensure information about risk, behaviour change and early detection is culturally appropriate and accessible
Address misconceptions or misinformation about cancer risk, behaviour change and early detection
Distinguish between increased risk of cancer and a cancer diagnosis and avoid language that catastrophises

Supportive care and communication actions related to risk and early detection of [cancer type] include: – list supportive care and communication actions related to risk and early detection specific to this cancer type; use a new row for each action
Allow adequate time for discussions about genetic risk and testing for cancer
Discuss the person’s right to not know genetic information and respect their preference
Use plain-language and offer a written summary of options for the person to take away
Refer people at familial or genetic risk for genetic counselling to ensure pre-and post-test support
Explore the meaning of genetic risk within the patient's cultural and belief framework
Communicate genetic risk clearly and compassionately, without catastrophising
Explain the implications for biological relatives in sensitive, non-coercive language
Empower people to make informed decisions about testing and family notification at their own pace – do not contact family members directly without the person’s consent
Assess emotional response to identification of familial risk and the impact on family dynamics and relationships, including for relatives who may be obligated to share genetic information
Support the person to decide whether, how and to whom to disclose genetic information and offer resources and support for family notification

Supportive care and communication actions related to familial / genetic risk of [cancer type] include: – list communication / supportive care actions about familial / genetic risk specific to this cancer type
Important psychosocial history and relevant medical history
Family history, current symptoms, medications and allergies
Results of current clinical investigations (e.g. imaging and pathology reports)
Results of all prior relevant investigations
Notification if an interpreter service is required.
Screen for distress and anxiety using a validated tool such as the NCCN Distress Thermometer and document the results

Provide referrals to appropriate sources of information, support and navigation via the Australian Cancer Nursing and Navigation Program (ACNNP): – Cancer Navigation Service ( Cancer Connect , 13 11 20 or Cancer Hub ) – Cancer Care Nursing Services ( Cancer Care Nurse Service ) <for prostate cancer OCP only add: or Prostate Cancer Specialist Nurses > – Specialist support services (via cancer-specific non-government organisations )
Consider involvement of a local care coordinator / navigator where available
Screen for practical barriers to attending specialist appointments and provide information about:
Encourage physical activity while the person waits for their appointment with the cancer specialist – Consider referral to an exercise physiologist if symptoms or deconditioning are present
Provide support to manage any physical symptoms including:
Action referrals to allied health or community support services to manage physical symptoms as required

Supportive care actions when investigating symptoms of [cancer type] include: – list supportive care actions relevant to investigation and referral of symptoms specific to this cancer type; use a new row for each action
Provide the person with verbal and written information about the referral and timeframe (who, why, when)
Consider the person’s preferred communication format, language and literacy and share this information as part of the specialist referral
Organise an interpreter if required
Provide clear instructions to contact the referring clinician if the specialist has not been in touch within the expected timeframe Document this instruction in the patient record
Explore options for telehealth consultation with the cancer specialist if appropriate
If the referrer is not the GP, send written communication to the person’s GP following the consultation
Notify the GP if the person does not attend their appointment with the cancer specialist

Communication actions when investigating symptoms of [cancer type] include: – list communication actions specific to investigation and referral of symptoms for this cancer type; use a new row for each action
Discuss requirements for genetic or genomic testing at the multidisciplinary team meeting
Consider referral to a molecular tumour board (where appropriate and available)
Consider the impact of timeframes for genetic or genomic testing on timelines for starting treatment
Ensure effective oncology–pathology collaborations to enable timely genetic and genomic testing
Order genetic tests as clinically indicated and in accordance with current evidence and guidelines
Consider costs of genetic testing – Medicare funds some germline tests via the Medicare Benefits Schedule – Other tests may be funded through state health systems
Take and document a family cancer history (three generations where possible) at diagnosis
Assess whether tumour pathological features suggest a hereditary predisposition
Consult eviQ Referral Guidelines to determine whether referral to a familial cancer service is warranted
Ensure pre-test counselling and informed consent before any germline test is ordered
Discuss Medicare Benefits Schedule funding and any out-of-pocket costs
If a pathogenic variant is identified, facilitate family risk notification and predictive testing for at-risk relatives through a familial cancer service
Document all discussions, decisions and referrals in the medical record
Determine required somatic tests are indicated
Review somatic testing results at the multidisciplinary team meeting to identify matched treatment options or clinical trial eligibility
Consider referral to a molecular tumour board if available
Discuss results and implications with the patient in plain language, including implications for family members
Document all testing decisions, results and treatment implications in the medical record
Send timely written communication to the GP about the person’s diagnosis and treatment plan
Invite the GP to participate in the multidisciplinary meeting (virtual attendance if available)
Discuss shared care arrangements and the GP's role during and after treatment

Screen for psychological distress at diagnosis using a validated tool such as the NCCN Distress Thermometer and document results – Activate referral pathways to psychology, social work or counselling as required

Provide referrals to appropriate sources of information, support and navigation via the Australian Cancer Nursing and Navigation Program (ACNNP): – Cancer Navigation Service ( Cancer Connect , 13 11 20 or Cancer Hub ) – Cancer Care Nursing Services ( Cancer Care Nurse Service ) <for prostate cancer OCP only add: or Prostate Cancer Specialist Nurses > – Specialist support services (via cancer-specific non-government organisations )
Identify whether the person is a primary caregiver and / or has access to family and carer support
Identify family and carer distress
Consider involvement of a local care coordinator / navigator where available
Assess and document baseline physical function and performance status
Assess weight status and discuss any implications for treatment planning; refer to a dietitian and/or exercise physiologist as appropriate

Consider completing malnutrition screening using a validated tool (e.g. Malnutrition Screening Tool ) and action referral to a dietitian if indicated (note that patients with a high BMI may also be malnourished)
Consider initiating a prehabilitation plan and refer to an exercise physiologist and/or physiotherapist as appropriate
Document smoking or vaping status – Offer brief cessation advice and offer referral to Quitline on 13 7848 if necessary – Prescribe pharmacotherapy if clinically appropriate

Discuss and document fertility implications of recommended treatment where appropriate: – provide contraception advice – discuss and document fertility preservation (including costs) with the person and relevant family or partner before any treatment starts – do not defer this conversation – refer to a fertility specialist if appropriate
Explore and document spiritual / pastoral care needs and make referral if appropriate

Supportive care actions during diagnosis and treatment planning for [cancer type] include: – list actions for supportive care at diagnosis specific to this cancer type; use a new row for each consideration
Initiate advance care planning and document preferences
Consider early palliative care referral

Supportive care actions during diagnosis and treatment planning for people with advanced [cancer type] include: – list actions for supportive care at diagnosis for people with advanced forms of this cancer; use a new row for each action
Explain the role and benefits of multidisciplinary care and the multidisciplinary team meeting to the patient
Obtain and document written or verbal consent from the person before presenting at the multidisciplinary meeting
Find out whether the person has a regular GP confirmed and if they do not, encourage them to establish one
Communicate the diagnosis and prognosis (if the person wants this information) clearly and using plain language
Answer questions clearly and openly and be respectful of the person's preferences for information, cultural beliefs, communication needs and capacity to understand
Provide the Guide to Best Cancer Care for the person’s cancer type and population-group
Discuss treatment options, including intent, risks, benefits and timeframes
Include discussion of supportive care considerations
Discuss costs and out of pocket expenses
Provide a written treatment care plan that includes:
Discuss the benefits of continued involvement of primary care during treatment for comorbidity management, health promotion and holistic care

Communication actions during diagnosis and treatment planning for [cancer type] include: – list communication actions related to diagnosis and treatment planning specific to this cancer type; use a new row for each action
Discuss treatment recommendations made by the multidisciplinary team with the patient and their family or carers
Obtain and document informed consent for treatment
Clearly outline the intent of treatment (curative, control or palliation)
Consider and discuss options for relevant clinical trials
Initiate early referral to palliative care services based on need and potential for benefit, not prognosis.
Emphasise the value of palliative care in improving symptom management and quality of life.
Reassess palliative care needs at each key clinical decision point.
Ensure that carers and families receive information, support and guidance about their role in palliative care. 37
Support the person and their family or carers to initiate advance care planning.
Proactively identify and document a person’s current or planned use of complementary therapies.
Assess each therapy for safety, efficacy and to identify any potential toxicity or drug interaction. 44
Communicate openly and without judgement when exploring the person’s reasons for wanting to use complementary therapies.
Consider both the evidence of benefit and the costs of therapies during discussions.

Where appropriate, discuss evidence-based integrative oncology approaches that may support symptom management, wellbeing and quality of life, such as physical activity, mindfulness-based interventions, yoga, acupuncture or oncology massage. 45

If a person expresses interest in using complementary therapies, consider referral to a multidisciplinary team member with relevant expertise (e.g. a clinical pharmacist, dietitian or psychologist) to help them reach an informed decision.
Two-way communication should cover:
Consider use of a Chronic Condition Management Plan (GPCCMP) (can be billed as an MBS item)
Screen for and document supportive care needs at the start of treatment and when treatment or treatment intent changes

Provide referrals to appropriate sources of information, support and navigation via the Australian Cancer Nursing and Navigation Program (ACNNP): – Cancer Navigation Service ( Cancer Connect , 13 11 20 or Cancer Hub ) – Cancer Care Nursing Services ( Cancer Care Nurse Service ) <for prostate cancer OCP only add: or Prostate Cancer Specialist Nurses > – Specialist support services (via cancer-specific non-government organisations )
Provide referrals to appropriate sources of information and support for people receiving palliative care e.g. via Palliative Care Australia
Screen for psychological distress using a validated tool such as the NCCN Distress Thermometer and document results – Activate referral pathways to psychology, social work or counselling as required
Assess family and carer needs and offer referrals as needed

Assess rehabilitation needs and refer for relevant allied health support as required; consider: – exercise prescription / referral to exercise physiologist or physiotherapist with cancer experience – nutritional status with referral to dietitian maintained or initiated if indicated – assessment of cancer-related fatigue assessed and provide information and self-management strategies
Assess financial and practical needs and provide information and referrals for support as required; consider: – financial impacts of treatment – legal requirements – isolation risks
Discuss and / or review and update advance care planning
Supportive care actions during treatment for [cancer type] include: – list supportive care actions during treatment specific to this cancer type; use a new bullet for each consideration
Discuss treatment intent, options and expected outcomes with the person and carer and provide written information/resources and referrals for professional and community support
Provide clear information on side effect management, self-management strategies and who to contact in an emergency
Support informed decision-making and encourage question prompt lists, audio recordings of consultations, and a support person at appointments
Discuss and document advance care planning
Maintain structured, timely two-way communication with the GP throughout treatment
Communication actions during treatment for [cancer type] include: – list communication actions during treatment specific to this cancer type; use a new row for each action

At the end of initial treatment, a designated member of the multidisciplinary team should meet with the patient to: – complete a needs assessment using a validated tool such as the NCCN Distress Thermometer and document results – activate referral pathways to psychology, social work or counselling as required – prepare and deliver a treatment summary – develop a survivorship care plan in partnership with the patient – agree and clearly document the follow-up model of care with the lead clinician, GP and relevant multidisciplinary team members – ensure the patient understands the rapid re-entry pathway and the specific symptoms of recurrence to report.
Provide copies of the treatment summary and survivorship care plan to the patient, their carer (if appropriate) and the person’s GP.
Consider opportunities to participate in clinical trials or research related to survivorship care and long-term health and wellbeing.

Recommendations for ongoing wellbeing and to reduce risk of recurrence:
Screen for fear of cancer recurrence, anxiety, depression and cognitive changes at follow-up appointments
Consider developing a mental health plan if required
Refer to psychology, social work or peer support as indicated
Identify financial hardship, return to work/study concerns and carer impacts early
Connect patients to financial counselling, social work and relevant support services

Referral to a fertility specialist for people of reproductive age who wish to conceive
Assess for signs of premature ovarian insufficiency or hypogonadism and refer to an endocrinologist or gynaecologist as appropriate

Consider use of a Chronic Condition Management Plan (GPCCMP) (can be billed as an MBS item)
Re-screen for supportive care needs using a validated tool such as the NCCN Distress Thermometer or CaSun and document the results
Assess for fear of cancer recurrence assessed and refer to relevant services
Refer the person to appropriate sources or information and support for financial, legal and employment concerns
Refer the person to appropriate sources of information and support for concerns related to intimacy, sexuality and body image
Provide the person with appropriate information and support for self-management, such as MyCarePlan .

Provide referrals to appropriate sources of information, support and navigation via the Australian Cancer Nursing and Navigation Program (ACNNP): – Cancer Navigation Service ( Cancer Connect , 13 11 20 or Cancer Hub ) – Cancer Care Nursing Services ( Cancer Care Nurse Service ) <for prostate cancer OCP only add: or Prostate Cancer Specialist Nurses > – Specialist support services (via cancer-specific non-government organisations )

Provide the person with information on the signs and symptoms of recurrent disease, secondary prevention and healthy living
Provide the person with contact details for the care team, and instructions on when to get in touch

Arrange appropriate staging investigations to confirm and characterise the extent of disease – Add key staging investigations for this cancer type
Re-biopsy where clinically indicated – Tumour biology can change, and receptor or molecular status may need to be re-evaluated to inform treatment planning
Refer or re-refer to the specialist multidisciplinary team without delay
Assess and document performance status and comorbidities to guide treatment planning
Initiate or reassess supportive care and psychosocial needs

Check the person's understanding of their diagnosis and prognosis and tailor the conversation to what they want to know
Hold sensitive, timely conversations about goals of care, advance care planning and the role of palliative care
Provide the person with contact details for the care team and instructions on when to get in touch
Establish regular, two-way communication with the person's GP, covering the treatment plan, prognosis, supportive and palliative care needs, and shared care arrangements

Communication actions for people with residual, recurrent or metastatic [cancer type] include: – list communication actions specific to people with residual, recurrent or metastatic forms of this cancer type; use a new row for each action
Ensure the person has an advance care directive in place
Ensure the person has been referred to palliative care
Discuss and document the person’s preferred place of care and death
Consider referral to home and community-based care, specialist community palliative care workers or community nursing as appropriate
Respond to any questions or information requests for voluntary assisted dying
Support care at home where this is the patient's preference and it is clinically and logistically feasible
Ensure the transition to the chosen care setting is planned, not reactive
Offer access to private physical spaces for gatherings as required
Coordinate with home-based community palliative care services, residential hospice, or inpatient palliative unit as appropriate
Undertake a specific needs assessment for families and carers and re-evaluate it regularly.

Ensure families and carers receive information, support and guidance about their caring role according to their needs and wishes, including practical guidance on day-to-day care and medications where care is provided at home.
Assess for anticipatory grief and the risk of prolonged grief, and refer to psychological, social work, pastoral or bereavement support as required.

Provide information about practical matters, including available support services, financial and legal considerations, and what to do after a death, and offer referral to bereavement support that continues after the person has died.
Actions to support families and carers of people with [cancer type] at end of life include: – <Optional> list actions or considerations for family and carer support specific to this cancer type
Keep the GP fully informed of major developments and involve them in end-of-life care planning
End-of-life care planning should be discussed with the GP so that the person’s needs and goals can be met in their preferred environment.
Assess physical, psychological, social, spiritual and existential needs using a validated tool and document the results, reassessing as needs change
Assess and actively manage symptoms, and refer to specialist palliative care, pain and allied health services as required
Confirm the person has an advance care directive and substitute decision-maker in place
Discuss and document the person’s preferred place of care and place of death
Identify and support practical, legal and financial needs, including a will, care of dependent children and insurance, superannuation or Centrelink claims
Assess carer and family needs and offer support, respite and referral, including for anticipatory grief, bereavement and support for dependent children

Provide referrals to appropriate sources of information, support and navigation via the Australian Cancer Nursing and Navigation Program (ACNNP): – Cancer Navigation Service ( Cancer Connect , 13 11 20 or Cancer Hub ) – Cancer Care Nursing Services ( Cancer Care Nurse Service ) <for prostate cancer OCP only add: or Prostate Cancer Specialist Nurses > – Specialist support services (via cancer-specific non-government organisations )
Provide referrals to appropriate sources of information and support for people receiving palliative care e.g. via Palliative Care Australia

Check the person’s understanding of their condition and prognosis and tailor conversations to what they and their family wish to know
Hold honest, compassionate conversations about goals of care, palliative care and the person’s preferred place of care and death, respecting cultural and spiritual needs

Provide the person, family and carers with contact details for the care team and palliative care service, including after-hours contacts, and clear information about what to do as death approaches and after a death

keyTableRows.rowLabel: Instructions for developers This template has been created to help authors of cancer-specific Optimal Care Pathways (OCPs) develop a high-quality and evidence-based resource that is consistent with the library of existing pathways. It contains two types of content: • core content that is standard across all OCPs and cannot be changed • editable content that must be completed or adapted for your cancer type. The template focuses on pathway steps for the OCP. Pathway steps are underpinned by the Principles for Optimal Cancer Care <hyperlink to be added>. Tips for success • Follow these instructions when developing your OCP. If you have any questions, contact Cancer Australia at OCPs@canceraustralia.gov.au • Keep content high level and scannable. Avoid lengthy narrative paragraphs. • Review the Principles for Optimal Cancer Care <hyperlink to be added> when developing content to avoid duplication and identify where cross-referencing is appropriate. Types of content in this template • Black text is core content that cannot be edited. This is standard content across all OCPs. • Text [highlighted in yellow] indicates words to be added / adapted for this cancer type / OCP. • Green boxes indicate content requiring developer input specific to this cancer type / OCP. Instructions are provided in green text. • Key considerations tables contain brief statements summarising what optimal care looks like at each step of the cancer pathway. Follow the green prompts to add any key cancer-specific considerations as new rows in these tables. • Checklists are actionable items for health professionals at key decision points. Follow the green prompts to add any cancer-specific actions as new rows in these lists. • Supportive care and communication sections: Each step has includes supportive care and communication considerations. Follow the green prompts to add cancer-specific content. • 'Find out more' boxes are curated links to guidelines and resources. These will appear on the digital hub with links from relevant sections. Follow the green prompts to add any specific resources for this cancer type and include the associated hyperlink. What you can and cannot change • Numbered headings and subheadings cannot be changed or reordered. This ensures consistency across the OCP library and aids with digitisation. • Additional third-level subheadings (i.e. non-numbered headings) can be added within sections. Consider additional sub-headings sparingly. • Sections can be removed where content is not relevant to this cancer type. Making changes • If you remove any sections or add any subheadings within sections, please indicate this when submitting the draft OCP content for review. • If you identify changes you believe should be made to core content, please list these separately when submitting draft OCP content. Suggestions will be considered intermittently as part of a centralised review process.

keyTableRows.rowLabel: The Principles for Optimal Cancer Care set the foundations for delivery of information, care and support for everyone who is at risk of and affected by cancer. Everyone in the healthcare system is responsible for delivering cancer care aligned to the Principles. Principles are relevant to all cancer types and all populations. Population-based OCPs may identify unique considerations for implementation for a particular population group.
keyTableRows.content: The Principles for Optimal Cancer Care set the foundations for delivery of information, care and support for everyone who is at risk of and affected by cancer. Everyone in the healthcare system is responsible for delivering cancer care aligned to the Principles. Principles are relevant to all cancer types and all populations. Population-based OCPs may identify unique considerations for implementation for a particular population group.
Equity <Link to Principle > <hyperlink to be added> Health equity in cancer outcomes is the absence of disparities for people with different levels of social advantage. 1

Person-centred care <Link to Principle > <hyperlink to be added> Person-centred care means informing and involving people in their care, and respecting and responding to their individual needs, preferences and values, as well as those of their families and carers. 2

Safe and quality care <Link to Principle> <hyperlink to be added> Safe and quality care means delivering the most appropriate and best-value care, while keeping people safe from preventable harm in the delivery of that care. 3

Multidisciplinary care <Link to Principle> <hyperlink to be added> Multidisciplinary care is an integrated team approach that involves all relevant health professionals discussing all relevant treatment options and making joint recommendations about treatment and supportive care plans that consider the individual characteristics and preferences of the person with cancer. 4

Supportive care <Link to Principle> <hyperlink to be added> Supportive care involves prevention and management of the adverse effects of cancer and its treatment, including management of physical and psychological symptoms and side effects across the cancer continuum. Supportive care aims to improve the quality of rehabilitation, secondary cancer prevention, survivorship, and end-of-life care. 5

Navigation and care coordination <Link to Principle> <hyperlink to be added> Navigation and care coordination are related person-centred interventions that aim to empower patients, families and carers affected by cancer to facilitate safe and timely access to optimal cancer-related care and support. 6
Communication <Link to Principle> <hyperlink to be added> Good communication is an essential part of cancer care and a responsibility of everyone involved in healthcare across the cancer continuum.7

Research and clinical trials <Link to Principle> <hyperlink to be added> Research and clinical trials generate evidence to improve understanding of cancer and to accelerate progress in prevention, detection, diagnosis, treatment, supportive care, survivorship care, palliative and end-of-life care. 8

keyTableRows.rowLabel: Optimal Care Pathways (OCPs) outline nationally agreed best practice across the entire cancer continuum. While the pathway steps are numbered in sequence, this does not mean the OCPs have to be used in a linear way. Optimal care for an individual is shaped by their cancer type, stage of disease and a range of personal characteristics and circumstances. Supportive care is a critical pathway-spanning step for the individual and their families and carers.

keyTableRows.rowLabel: To ensure safe and high-quality delivery of radiation therapy, health services should have these features: • linear accelerator (LINAC) capable of image-guided radiation therapy (IGRT) • dedicated computed tomography (CT) planning • access to magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and positron emission tomography (PET) imaging • automatic record-verify of all radiation treatments delivered • a treatment planning system • trained medical physicists, radiation therapists and nurses with radiation therapy experience • coordination for combined therapy with systemic therapy, especially where facilities are not co-located • participation in audits Australian Clinical Dosimetry Service • an incident management system linked with a quality management system.
keyTableRows.content: To ensure safe and high-quality delivery of radiation therapy, health services should have these features: • linear accelerator (LINAC) capable of image-guided radiation therapy (IGRT) • dedicated computed tomography (CT) planning • access to magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and positron emission tomography (PET) imaging • automatic record-verify of all radiation treatments delivered • a treatment planning system • trained medical physicists, radiation therapists and nurses with radiation therapy experience • coordination for combined therapy with systemic therapy, especially where facilities are not co-located • participation in audits Australian Clinical Dosimetry Service • an incident management system linked with a quality management system.

keyTableRows.rowLabel: To ensure safe and high-quality delivery of systemic therapy, health services should have these features: • a clearly defined path to emergency care and advice after hours • access to diagnostic pathology including basic haematology and biochemistry, and imaging • cytotoxic drugs prepared in a pharmacy with appropriate facilities • occupational health and safety guidelines regarding handling of cytotoxic drugs, including preparation, waste procedures and spill kits 47 47 eviQ 2024 Accessed July 2026 Clinical procedure - hazardous drug spill management • guidelines and protocols to for delivery and extravasation • coordination for combined therapy with radiation therapy, especially where facilities are not co-located • appropriate molecular pathology access.

devBoxPrompts.promptText: • Green boxes indicate content requiring developer input specific to this cancer type / OCP. Instructions are provided in green text.

• Key considerations tables contain brief statements summarising what optimal care looks like at each step of the cancer pathway. Follow the green prompts to add any key cancer-specific considerations as new rows in these tables.
• Checklists are actionable items for health professionals at key decision points. Follow the green prompts to add any cancer-specific actions as new rows in these lists.
• Supportive care and communication sections: Each step has includes supportive care and communication considerations. Follow the green prompts to add cancer-specific content.

• 'Find out more' boxes are curated links to guidelines and resources. These will appear on the digital hub with links from relevant sections. Follow the green prompts to add any specific resources for this cancer type and include the associated hyperlink.

Include in final version We acknowledge Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people as the Traditional Custodians of Country throughout Australia. We pay our respects to Elders, past and present. We celebrate the ongoing connections of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples to Country, culture, community, family and tradition and recognise these as integral to health, healing and wellbeing. We acknowledge great diversity among Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, and the contribution of the many voices, knowledge systems and experiences that guide all efforts to create a culturally safe and responsive cancer system that is equitable to all. This Optimal Care athway was formally endorsed by the Cancer and Population Screening Committee (CAPS) following advice from Cancer Australia’s National Cancer Expert Group (NCEG). Formal endorsement by the CAPS Committee acknowledges the importance of this Optimal Care Pathway and the responsibility of the health system to deliver care in an appropriate, culturally safe, responsive and coordinated manner to ensure access and that optimal health outcomes are experienced by all Australians.
